Berwickshire
BER-ik-shur
n. (the Scottish border county of the Merse, birthplace of Duns Scotus, whose name became the English word dunce)
From Berwick, Old English bere wic, the barley farm; the county retains the name though the town of Berwick passed to England in 1482.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Berwickshire is the Scottish border county of the fertile plain called the Merse, running from the Lammermuirs down to the Tweed, and it keeps the name of a town that has been English since 1482. Its village of Duns gave the medieval church one of its greatest intellects. John Duns Scotus, born there about 1266, became the Subtle Doctor, a Franciscan who taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne, defended the immaculate conception of the Virgin, argued the primacy of the will over the intellect, and built an apparatus of formal distinctions so fine that his successors could not agree what he had meant. When the humanists and then the Reformers turned on the schoolmen, Scotus became the type of the subtlety that proves nothing, and his followers were called Dunses; from that the English word dunce descends, which is the most ironic fate in the history of learning. In 1639 the covenanting army mustered on Duns Law in the same parish, and the county was afterward solidly Presbyterian. The dictionary records both facts about Duns, and holds that the disgrace of a great mind is a warning about method rather than about ability.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a schoolman as one versed in the niceties of the schools; subtlety as refinement or nicety of distinction; a dunce as a dullard; doctrine as that which is taught; and reading as the public perusal of Scripture.

expand to see more

SCHOOLMAN, n. A man versed in the niceties of academical disputation, or of school divinity.

SUBTLETY, n. Thinness; fineness; refinement; extreme acuteness; cunning; artifice.

DUNCE, n. A person of weak intellect; a dullard; one who is incapable of learning.

DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true.

READING, n. The act of perusing; a public lecture or recitation; the study of books.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

1Ti 4:13 — "Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine."

Modern Corruption

Scottish border county of the Merse whose village of Duns produced John Duns Scotus about 1266 and whose name became the English word dunce, and where the covenanting army mustered on Duns Law in 1639.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is scholastic method as it had become by the fourteenth century, and the dictionary is careful about the charge. The objection is not to distinctions, nor to logic, nor to the use of reason in divinity; Reformed orthodoxy made heavy use of all three and the Reformers were trained schoolmen themselves. The objection is to a method that spun distinctions out of distinctions without a controlling text, so that a question was settled by whoever could draw the finer line, and the whole of it rested on authorities and traditions the Scriptures had never established. Paul warns that God deliberately chose a method that would look foolish to such men, since “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).

The second paragraph names the test that was missing and the irony that followed. Isaiah supplies the control: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Where that control is absent, apparatus multiplies and settles nothing, and Paul describes the result as impressive and empty, having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23). The remedy he prescribes to a young minister is almost crude by comparison and is in three words: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). Scotus was not a dunce; he was one of the ablest men of his age, and his name became a byword for stupidity because he spent that ability on a method that could not be checked. The dictionary enters the fact as the sharpest available warning to clever men in theology, and notes that three and a half centuries later the ploughmen of the same parish were mustering on Duns Law for a confession they could state in a page.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek moria (G3472), foolishness; Hebrew torah (H8451), law; Greek anagnosis (G320), reading.

expand to see more

Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness, absurdity; “by the foolishness of preaching”, 1 Corinthians 1:21.

Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom, skill, learning; “the world by wisdom knew not God”, 1 Corinthians 1:21.

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-chosen worship; “a shew of wisdom in will worship”, Colossians 2:23.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek anagnosis (G320) — a reading, the public reading of scripture; “give attendance to reading”, 1 Timothy 4:13.

Usage

"“by the foolishness of preaching” (1Co 1:21) — a method God chose against the schools."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the control the schoolmen lacked."

"“give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) — three words against an apparatus."
